utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Your Honours, good morning. Good morning counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franjic. We have met before once but for the record and for your memory, my name is Michael Blaxill, and I'm one of the Prosecuting counsel engaged in this case. So I do have a few questions for you, sir, as a result of the evidence you gave here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, up to and including the 15th of April, 1993, you worked visiting the Hotel Vitez on an almost daily basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In the performance of those duties did you wear civilian clothing, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you, in fact, wearing civilian clothes, like a suit and tie or something like, that on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, at that time, you said that you were not in any way a soldier, or a member of the military, HVO, or anything of that nature, is that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was not an organised soldier if we leave aside the village patrols, because we saw what was happening. The Serbs were already attacking Sarajevo, the village of Ravno, and strange things were going on. So the village patrols were organised so that we could protect our families and our homes, but I was not organised as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So in connection with your involvement in the village guards, did you possess any form of uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was a uniform I often borrowed from others, and then people managed to get things. But if anyone had a uniform, he could wear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you yourself purchase any kind of uniform clothing, perhaps camouflage jacket or trousers or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You possessed these items of uniform, did you, prior to the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that uniform include both the trousers and a sort of camouflage jacket or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I had only a jacket and a cap of items of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you attach any form of badge or patch or insignia to any of those, to the cap or to the jacket?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, sometimes. Sometimes you would put on some kind of patch, but there were no official patches. They changed very often because there was no real organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So very specifically, sir, did you put any badge on any part of your uniform clothing, and if so, would you describe that badge to it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there was no patch on my jacket and on my cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, if that's correct, perhaps of a sew-on type of patch. What about a badge? Did you have any kind of metal badge you clipped onto your clothing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the Croatian coat of arms without the part that is on the coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia. It was just the checkerboard coat of arms, and I bought it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you possess any weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you say what weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you carry that pistol when performing village guard duty?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you possess any other weapon than the pistol, like perhaps a shotgun or hunting rifle or something?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any other weapons. I was not a hunter, so I did not have a hunting rifle. Not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you left the Hotel Vitez on the afternoon of the 15th of April, 1993, what was the atmosphere at the hotel like? Was it quiet, was everything normal, or had you noticed anything like a tension in the atmosphere amongst the military staying there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nothing usual. It was a usual working day for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay. So you went home, and later that evening you say you noticed soldiers outside your apartment? I believe that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not in the evening but in the afternoon at around 3.00 p.m. It was not next to my apartment but below my family house, and they were moving along the main road and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you say you saw these armed men moving along the road and they then set up some form of barricade, I believe you say, facing the Croatian part of town. Is that roughly correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not facing. It was a barricade, a roadblock, to monitor the passage of people and vehicles along that road and check who was passing through. It was set up to separate the Croatian population from the Muslim population, and I was unfortunate enough to -- my house was in the Muslim part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. Had you encountered such things before? I believe you say they had put up barricades and things like this before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not just once, an untold number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you, on more than one occasion, had to pass through such a barricade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I did pass through such barricades quite often, depending on my own estimate of the situation. If I thought it was dangerous, I would walk over the meadows to avoid any kind of misunderstandings or problems. However, I think it was in late 1992, in October or November, when they set up this roadblock, and I tried to take my family in my car to my brothers who were in the part of the village that was inhabited by a majority Croatian population. Then they asked to see my identity card. They searched me. They shot in my direction. They fired shots in my direction and very unpleasant things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On those occasions, sir, that you went through such checkpoints, were you normally clad in your civilian clothing or were you ever wearing parts of that uniform you say you had acquired?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very often it was in civilian clothes, but the time they fired shots in my direction I was wearing the jacket and cap but not carrying any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say that later on, you felt that the situation did not look safe, so I believe you sent members of your family to your brother's house, where you felt they would be safer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wasn't me that took them. I sent them there on their own, and I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were you then the only person in your apartment at that time, after they had gone?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My relative was with me. He arrived. I rang him up on the telephone, and he came to my house. It was in the evening, around 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., when he arrived. And I was alone after 5.00, half past 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you said that you subsequently left the apartment yourself and went to another property that you had, your old house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but that was at around 2200, 2300 hours. I went out of my house-- as soon as they set up the roadblock, I went out and -- I went in and out of the house. I walked around. And then, when it got dark, and there was no electricity, I thought it was very dangerous to be alone there, so I called my relative. He arrived, and at about 2200, 2300 hours -- well, up to that time, we walked around the house, the farm buildings, and that was all some 10 metres away from the road, where there were about 15 soldiers who were probably trying to intimidate us. I don't know exactly what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you said you were outside in the early part of the evening from time to time, did any soldiers give you a hard time? Did anybody stop you, or did anybody harass you in any way?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they couldn't stop me, because I was not on the road. I was some ten metres away from the road. They did not approach my house because they probably knew that they couldn't do it just like that, because each of us has his dignity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But were you at times visible to these soldiers? And you're saying a distance of some 10 metres from the road; I mean, could they see you from where they were?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because my house is on a slope, so they couldn't see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Which house are we referring to there? This is your apartment, the one you had been in earlier that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you just remind me, please, because I'm perhaps a little confused here. What made you then leave that family home and go to the other house, of your relative?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, because in the immediate vicinity of my house, about 10 metres below my house, in my estimate there were 10, 15, or 20 members of the Muslim army. They were having a heated discussion. About 30 or 50 metres away there was the roadblock, and there were some 30 or 40; I couldn't count them. So I felt unsafe, and so we went to my old house, which was on a hill overlooking the place where my family house was. It was some -- a little more than 100 metres away. I thought we would feel much safer there. It would be easier for us to watch out and see if anyone was approaching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What were you wearing when you left your family home to go to that other house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was wearing the camouflage jacket and the jeans.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you wear your cap, military cap?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did the cap still have the Croatian badge attached to it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not on the cap, but on the pocket on my left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you carrying a weapon when you left your family home to move to the other house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, perhaps it's my confusion here to understand the situation, but you've told us that generally speaking, in your previous encounters with Muslim army troops, the only occasions you'd been shot at were when you were wearing the camouflage uniform. Wasn't that inviting trouble, to wear that uniform to go up to your other house? Wouldn't you have been better off in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I think not, because I could tell you about a number of times when I was harassed while wearing civilian clothes. These were provocations, because how can you explain this? If you set up a roadblock 30 metres away from my house, and I arrive as a civilian in my private car, and they search me, and they ask to see my identity papers, and these are people with whom I grew up; is this normal? So uniform or no uniform, they did the same things. It was a system of intimidation. They fired shots at my family home. They fired shots at the light bulb if it was left on at night, and these things happened many times. They wanted me to put my lights out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But I believe I'm right if I recall you saying here this morning, sir, that the times that you had been shot at were the ones when you were wearing your camouflage rather than when you were wearing civilian clothes. That is a difference, isn't it, sir, being shot at?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't think the reason they shot at me was my camouflage uniform. I think the reason was the improper behaviour of the Muslim soldiers, and I answered back. When they asked to see my identity papers, my identity card, I wouldn't show it to them. I refused to open the boot of my car. I opposed them. In the end, I did open it, and there were only tools there and a spare tire. So it was their attempt to hurt my dignity, to upset me, and I opposed them. So I don't think that the uniform had anything to do with it, with the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay, sir, thank you. Now, you went and spent the rest of the night in that particular house, and I recall, to cut a longer story short, that in the morning you made your way to a predominantly Croat village and from there to Hotel Vitez. Does that summarise briefly your movements?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, sir, you spent the night at that other house of yours, and I think you've described it as a fairly sleepless night. You were in part sort of guarding the property and watching out for what was going on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you in fact see any kind of unusual activity by those Muslim troops during that night?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that was unusual. It was unusual for them to set up the roadblock. As I said, they'd done it before, but if there was an incident in Gornji Vakuf or Novi Travnik. The reasons why they set up these roadblocks, I don't know, but it was unusual for there to be 50 or 70 people in front of my house. That was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you certainly suspected something somewhat intimidating, let us say, because of the sheer numbers of those troops and the fact that there is usually a roadblock, after an incident, somewhere; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I was not expecting anything bad because such things had happened before, and we would spend the night not sleeping, and guarding my house, and then in the morning I would go to work again. But that morning, things happened. What happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And, of course, in order to be where you were, you had had to leave your other family home down near the barricade and near the soldiers, you had had to leave that empty, I presume, overnight?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, when you and your relative moved to the other house, your wife and child had already gone, so I presume you left that family home empty overnight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean my family house? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you eventually made your way, as you say, to the Hotel Vitez, and you believe it was somewhere around 6.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I left my parents' old house at about half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you left the old house, could you at that time hear the sound of any artillery shelling or of small-arms gunfire?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only detonations could be heard. Shells were falling. There were detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As you got closer to the hotel, did you start to hear the sound of small-arms fire? Rifles, or pistols, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long do you think it took you to walk from the house down to the village, and then from there to Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, how long -- I really couldn't time it or anything, nor is it logical. Perhaps I need a little bit more, or perhaps one needed to be more cautious going from that family house to that locality with the Croat population, which is called Toljusici, isn't it. And from Toljusici, well, it could be 15, 20 minutes. I don't really know. It can't be more than 800 metres, perhaps a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Hotel Vitez, I think you've described a scene of some chaos. Is that a correct description?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So there were people running around all over the place, a lot of shouting and general milling around. Would you say that's a fair description?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not around the hotel, within the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, I mean within the hotel building. Did you, at any point there, physically check to see what time it was, what time of day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What shall I say? I always have a watch on my wrist and one does look at it now and again. It could have been around quarter past six, half past six. Listen, it was seven or eight years ago. I really can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We understand that, Mr. Franjic. Sir, you then saw Mr. Vlado Santic in the sort of reception area in the hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And we've heard your description of a very brief and on his part dismissive encounter which presumably lasted only a matter of seconds or a minute. Would you say that's right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At that point you decided you would leave the hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't decide. It must have been spontaneous, because I was afraid. I had nothing to look for there. I saw that my staff wasn't there so I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How did you leave the building, sir? Which direction did you take?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the hotel towards the department store which was behind the hotel, in the direction of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's my fault, Mr. Franjic. I didn't ask that question very well. Inside the hotel, what exit did you take to leave it? That's what I meant to ask you. I'm sorry, I was unclear.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The main exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then, in fact, made your way towards home or something like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, you do recall, do you not, meeting an investigator from the Tribunal, certainly some weeks ago now?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like just to quote a few words that were recorded when you and he spoke, and indeed Defence counsel and myself were also present. If this is correct from the transcript, you said: "I just walked through the restaurant to check, to make sure none of the staff was there, and since there wasn't anybody, I just left and I went out through the other exit, through the coffee shop, going by the fence of the terrace so I would be more covered, more protected." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So which is correct, because you've just said to me that you went out the main exit but you've now confirmed that you told us previously that you went out through the coffee shop exit. Could you verify for the court, please, which is the correct direction?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Both are correct. When I went through the restaurant, I entered the office and saw that none of the staff were there. So I came into the coffee shop, because from the office there is a door to the coffee shop. So through the coffee shop I went to the main entrance, but not by the terrace, but I walked next to the fence of the terrace and I went by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may just have a moment, Your Honours. I'm just wondering, Your Honours, if, in fact, the Defence exhibit, the photographs of the front of the Hotel Vitez, the last Defence exhibit, I really would like to try and locate where the terrace is in relation to the building. I think that might assist us. I think it's D10. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, looking at that photograph in front of you, would you recognise that as of the front of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't know if it is possible with this photograph, but can you say, looking at the front of the hotel, where is the terrace that you refer to? You referred to a terrace and a fence. Could you sort of indicate where they would be in relation to this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, you could do it on the machine to your right. That will actually pick up the pointer for the camera, for the rest of us. Could you use the pointer? Oh, it's -- could you point again just for clarity, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much indeed. Now, I'd like to return to the point of what Mr. Santic was doing when you had that brief encounter with him. Was he with other people?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlado was standing. He was in the lobby, between the reception desk and the restaurant. As I have said, my impression was that he was panicky, that he was very, very agitated. Yes. He was indicating something with his hands, but around there in the lobby there were more military policemen milling around. Whether he was giving instructions to them, perhaps guidelines, what kind of a conversation there was and if there was any kind of conversation, I do not know. I simply could not register something like that. I was really focusing on what I wanted to know, that is, to find out what was going on, and I tried to do it through Vlado and I got the answer that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you'd known Mr. Vlado Santic for some considerable time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So do you know what role or function he performed in the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not quite. I believe he was a superior. He was a commander of something, but what rank, what level, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, Mr. Santic was wearing a uniform, was he?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did he have any other distinguishing equipment like a particular kind of belt or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I think he was dressed as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was he carrying or wearing any form of weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So when you left the hotel, can you say where you went, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to Vinko Miskovic's house, because my family was there in the cellar. Vinko Miskovic's cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you return at all to the Hotel Vitez during the rest of that day, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when you next went back to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was some six, seven, or eight days later. Not to the Hotel Vitez but it was when I came back to Vitez again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When did you, in fact, or have you, in fact, ever been back to the hotel since that day, the 16th of April, and if so, when was your first visit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was sometime -- I don't know exactly. If you want me to be specific I really can't, but I know that I went to Vitez some seven or eight days later, and to the hotel it could have been perhaps 10 or 12 days later. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for Mr. Franjic. I would like, if I may, to tender the transcript that has been made of the interview that was undertaken. I have referred to a section of it. I think though, as I would always argue, if people want a part of a document to go in we always argue it should be the full thing. So I would like to tender that in evidence. It hasn't been served today on Mr. Pavkovic, because, of course, he received a copy in the course of preceding weeks, as well as a copy of the audiotapes that were taken at the time, and we were all present at the interview. So unless my friend has any objection, I would ask Your Honours to receive that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Date, can we have a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The date of the interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I should remember clearly; I was there. But it was the 10th of March, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: None, Mr. President. I can confirm that it was indeed on the 10th of March, 1993 (sic).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, not '93, '99. I did say 10th of March, 1993, but I meant 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can we receive this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I do not have a copy in any condition to hand to Your Honours, I'm afraid. May we leave it till the break? And then sufficient copies will be submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 372.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should now ask the usher to get D10/6, the one that we just saw, so as to round off the story that the witness has commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, you pointed out to us the route that you took when you left the hotel on the 16th of April, and you said that you went out through the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I only showed the terrace. I did not show the main exit, nor nobody asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did say that you went out through the main exit. Here on this photograph, we see two exits, and they more or less look the same, except that over one of them, it says "Hotel Vitez." Which one did you use to get out? Which was the main entrance, to your mind, at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exit number 1, because exit number 2 was locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the lower part of this hotel, were there yet other exits, on the other side, which served for different purposes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And those exits, were they locked, too, like the 1 and the 2?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All of them except for number 1 had to be locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, will you show us, when you reached the terrace which you had just showed to us, where did you go? You were inside the hotel, and you headed for the main -- to the main exit, and where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said towards the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, we're still in the hotel. You reached the terrace, which is inside the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. Right next to the terrace is the coffee shop, the cafeteria. So from the office I entered the cafeteria, went through the cafeteria, then entered the hallway which links these two exits, passed by this exit and came out of the main exit, because it was the safest next to the exit two, because there were some small fir trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please show us on the photograph? Will you please show us on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So here, this glass space here, this is where the cafeteria is (indicating). This is the fence of the terrace (indicating), and roughly here (indicating). But inside the hotel is the kitchen, office, and all the other work premises. So through the restaurant, I went into the office, then came to the cafeteria, that is, the door into the cafeteria, (indiscernible) exit, depends, of course. Went through the cafeteria, reached this door and the hallway between these two entrances (indicating), went through it and came out here (indicating), and then went like this (indicating), because this was the safest. There is yet another part of the hotel, where there are hotel rooms, and it was quite welcome at the time because it provided a shelter from the bullets and whatever. So I walked here (indicating), walked again past the fence of the terrace, and we have some pine trees, and they are also a good shelter. Between the fence and these pine trees, I went towards the department store, which is around the corner, and then got to the street between the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I understand which route you took to get out of the hotel and away from the hotel. I think this should be clear now.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic, there is one matter which isn't clear, and it may be to do with the interpretation, I'm not sure. The witness said that, looking at the photograph D10/6, that the windows to the left were the windows of the cafeteria. Now, is that the coffee shop? Perhaps we can clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Judge May, perhaps the witness could explain it. He is much more familiar with it than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the coffee and tea room, or the cafeteria, or the coffee shop, or what is it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the cafeteria (indicating), and there is a cafeteria -- a coffee shop on the other side that is on the other side of the coffee room, of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So inside the hotel, there is an area which you went through to see if any of your staff were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you say this door was locked, door 2 was locked. You did not find there any one of your employees, and you headed very quickly towards the main entrance and then onward, as you have already described?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's still not clear. Mr. Franjic, you referred, when you were interviewed, to the investigator, as going through the coffee shop -- I'm sorry, leaving the hotel by the exit to the coffee shop. Now, where is the coffee shop in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not say that I left the hotel through the coffee -- through the cafe. I said through the coffee shop of the hotel, the coffee room, so to speak, because at that time one could not go into the cafe, as the waiter on duty there, he locks the door between the office -- that is, the waiter's working space -- and this coffee shop. And at that time nobody could go into it, and I couldn't, because -- and I never had any keys to anything anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we see, on the photograph, the windows of the cafeteria. Where in relation to that is the coffee shop?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if you have the photograph of the hotel from the other side, then I would like to see it, and then I will be able to show you. It is very difficult for me to show you where exactly here, but it is opposite to these windows that you see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, so you left through the main entrance simply because it was the only one which was not locked?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to that moment when you came across Vlado Santic in the lobby of the hotel near the receptionists. You told us it was a very brief encounter, and it was not very pleasant. You said you felt ill at ease, and you started immediately towards the coffee shop and then you took that route that we just talked about, and went out?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I -- no, I mean this is the substance of what you told us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not start immediately towards the coffee shop. I said that I went through the restaurant and then to the office to see in the coffee shop whether there was any one there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was trying to simplify it. You told us that it all took a very short time and when you left the hotel, where was Vlado Santic at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. When I entered the restaurant and went through it, Vlado was still in the lobby behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you left the hotel and walked past the hotel, hiding?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we assume that Vlado Santic followed on your steps, that is, out of the hotel, would you, since you were moving very fast, would you have been able to see him in that area in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, like anyone else not only Vlado Santic, any person who would be in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And as you were coming out of the hotel, did you see anyone in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw a soldier taking his position there, and a couple of military policemen, perhaps, there at the entrance were going out, some were coming in. That was roughly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Franjic, you told us you were not a member of any organised military formation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right. Not in the beginning of the conflict, except for the village guards, if one can call it an army formation, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in is the period of time prior to the conflict. Why did you then go out to acquire that military outfit that you mentioned today?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what shall I tell you? For some reasons of safety, I should say. We all watched -- listened to the media, we all knew what was going on, and I suppose I would have bought something more substantial had I had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was referring only to your outfit, to your clothes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, why did I buy it? Well, because it was a camouflage uniform, and I guess I felt that if the need arose, I could hide. I would be better protected. But to be quite honest, it was quite in; camouflage uniforms were rather in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted you to tell us to better describe this period of time when those ethnic emotions were also rather hot. That was also a way to show your national feelings?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I should like to ask you something about the badge that you wore on that jacket. You told us that you also had it on the 15th of April, 1993. So my question is: Is that a badge which related you to an army unit which epitomised, which stood for your membership in a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, come, no. It is simply -- probably I just wanted to express my, my ethnic feeling, my feeling of belonging to a particular ethnicity. It was a matter of pride to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But was that a badge that one wore only with -- that went only with the army clothes, or did people wear it simply to express their ethnic feelings, and so people would put it on their civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was that kind that I could afford at the time. I had bought them for my children, but sometimes I wore it simply to express, to give vent to my pride, to give a demonstration of my dignity of my ethnic pride, things like that. But, yes, there were also those real gem, and if I may call them that, badges which did indicate a membership in a particular formation, but I did not have that kind of badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Today, in response to the Prosecutor's question as to what the situation was like in the hotel on the 15th of April, 1993, you answered that the situation was normal. Thus you stated the situation was normal. What did you mean by that? Did you mean that it was as it was during the previous days?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A usual working day. There were no problems. There were no incidents. So all of it was the usual thing for me, normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So on the 15th of April, 1993 it is not only on the 15th of April, 1993, that the military were there, so it is not only on the 15th of April, 1993, that the military were there at the hotel, they were there considerably earlier right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, yes, 1992, as far back that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said to us today that when you left your old house you had a pistol as well.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why you had obtained this weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Why? Probably for safety reasons. I probably didn't get it to show off. I obviously thought I needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you feel threatened?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I felt threatened. I told the Prosecutor all the things that happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't wish us to repeat all of that. You said that.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity of telling you about some uglier things that happened but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: The presence of numerous military men in front your house on the 15th of April, in the evening, is that the reason why you then sent away your family, your wife, to a safer place?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand your question right. I had other things on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it fear for your family that evening, on the 15th of April, 1993, when you saw all those soldiers in front of your house, was fear the reason why you sent your family to a safer place?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was the main reason, because now, when I asked you to repeat your question, I was thinking about a family situation that happened. It was a tragedy that occurred and that's why I sent my family away. One of my sons was already staying with my brothers, and I sent the other one with my wife that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Franjic. I have another question. In response to the Prosecutor's question, you said that that morning, on the 16th of April, 1993, Vlado Santic was dressed as usual; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please, tell me very briefly, what did you mean when you said "as usual"? What did that mean for you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "As usual"? I was referring to Vlado. That's the way I would see him. He was wearing a camouflage uniform, a belt, a pistol. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how you saw Vlado dressed during those previous days when you would come there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. We have no questions for the witness. Mr. Franjic, thank you so much for testifying yesterday and today. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic, are you going to call Mr. Groenewold?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewold should be here by now, and he should be ready to enter the courtroom. May I say, Mr. President, that I believe that his questioning, as we stated a few days ago, will be very brief, and I believe that we will be able to take care of the other two witnesses today, character witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I agree with you. It should be extremely brief. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewold, good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Witness. I would like to introduce myself to you first. My name is Petar Pavkovic. I'm an attorney at law and I'm Defence counsel for Vladimir Santic. I don't know whether you can hear the interpretation of what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the court now? Could you give the court your name and surname, your age, your occupation, and your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: My name is Wout Groenewold. I'm 40 years old. I'm a director of school in Amsterdam, and I'm living in Zaandam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the place where you live? You were not understood exactly by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I live in Zaandam. It's near Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were the principal of a school, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether, during the school year of '92/'93, you were also principal of this school or, to put this better, for how long have you been principal of that school?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, if we now go back to 1992 and 1993, at that time did you meet a family that came from Bosnia, a family of refugees, the family of Stipo Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances under which you met them?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: The first person of the family I met was the woman. She came to my school and she applied her children. Well, her oldest daughter, because the son Petar was still too young. Then he came too. I don't know the word in English Peuterspeelzaal, because he was not four years old yet, and that was in December '92. They came from a refugee camp, I think, somewhere near Rosmala (phoen), I think to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Since then you would see them from time to time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you would meet them, would they be accompanied by a person who would help them understand things better?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes. The mother had a friend, girlfriend, who was a -- I don't know whether she was really a friend or perhaps she only lived near her, and she was the mother of her pupil who already left our school. I tried to remember the maiden name but that's difficult. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I would say that this is Mrs. Hume, would that name ring a bell? No?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Is that her maiden name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Hume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mrs. Dasovic?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I think that's right. She had two daughters? Usually I better know the children than the parents. Dasovic. I think that's right. Do you have an address? She lived Knollendamstraat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it here with me now but I think that what you have said is sufficient. Please tell me, sir, after you met the mother of these children, did you get to meet their father as well, her husband?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes. I met him several times, not often. Mostly the mother brought the children to school, and I think the first time I met the father, that was after a few months, I think, perhaps in January or February. But he usually did not bring the children and I did not visit their home, but sometimes I -- or we met in the street and they said hello because I knew his face, but we never spoke in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, did you always know when parents brought children to school? Would you always see them? You are the principal of the school.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Not always, but usually when the door opens and the children come in, I'm at the door, and I'm there till someone needs me. Sometimes the parents want to talk to me or -- well, sometimes there are problems, but usually I open the door and then the children come in, and the small children are brought by the parents. Well, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have several teachers in your school?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm going to pronounce this right, but Mrs. Kolk, is she also a teacher in your school?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is she still employed in your school?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: She's still employed, and she was the teacher of Petar, the younger one, but that was from, I think, '93, August '93, because up to that time he was too young. Perhaps even later, because I think Petar -- Petar's birthday was about -- somewhere in November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, we're talking about such very young children -- actually, I'd like to withdraw this question. You said that you did not visit the Alilovic family. According to your school rules and according to customary behaviour there, would the teacher go to see the house of the parents of the children so that she would see how these children lived? Could you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Usually children are visited once in two years. So not every year, once in two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On such occasions are teachers supposed to send a report to you, as principal of the school, stating what they noticed on the occasion of such visits?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Only if there are things that I should know, things that are special, which could be important for other things outside of school, but usually no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are there rules and regulations here in the Netherlands that make it binding upon you to keep documents in schools for a certain number of years?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I have to keep some documents. Most documents for, I think, five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So today, even if we wanted to obtain something from that period, obviously we could not get any such reports if they were significant at the time.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: No, that's right. I tried to find things from days back, but in '93 or '94 we got a computer system for the first time, and since that time I have some records but then only records of children who are present or not present, and all I found was a subscription only of the oldest daughter, not from the son. That's not an excuse, but the school had a fusion -- is that an English word -- then together an old school in '95, and then the administration was totally changed. So before August '95, I have almost nothing more. Nothing is left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now what Stipo Alilovic looked like physically? Could you describe him to me physically?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Tall man, grey hair, but he changed a lot the last years, because you know, of course, he died of cancer. So he became -- how do you call it? Smaller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "Gaunt" is the word, "gaunt."

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I'll try to remember. He had very strong eyes, but for -- if you've got ten pictures, I think I can pick him out, but to describe is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a beard?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes, grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: During all the time you knew him, up until his death, did he always wear a beard?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I think not in the beginning, but later he wore a beard, short.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Stipo died. Can you remember which year this was?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: That must have been -- I think it was in March, April '95, because Emma was still in school and she left in August '95, somewhere there. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that before he died he was sick, that he had cancer. Can you remember whether at that time he was already afflicted by this illness in '92, '93, '94? Was he an exhausted person? You said that he was gaunt, that his cheeks were sallow. So what was the impression one would get, that he was a sickly person and in poor physical shape? I don't know how to put this. If you know anything about this, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I think in '92/'93 -- he was not a fat man, he was never a fat man, but in '92/'93, he was -- I forgot that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Gaunt.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Gaunt, as in '94/'95. Then he became more gaunt than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Stipo drank?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Drank?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: I don't know. He smoked a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall be finished soon, but I would like to ask for a photograph to be shown to the witness. It is included in document C10. So can the witness then state whether that is a photograph of the person that he talked about today?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us who you see on this photograph? Is that the person you described today as Stipo Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Franck Terrier, and I represent the Prosecution in this case. I should like to ask you a few questions. What concerns this particular stage of the proceedings is the following question: Is it possible to establish beyond any doubt, and without an error, that Stipo Alilovic never left Amsterdam on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of April, 1993? So the question is very precise. Can you help us to resolve it or not?

utterances.speaker: WOUT GROENEWOLD
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for the witness. Mr. Groenewold, thank you so much for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And I suggest that we take now a coffee break, a recess now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, I assume, since these are two character witnesses, the testimony can be fairly brief, so if you would get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This witness will be brief in his statement. The other one will be a little longer, but I hope I shall be able to comply with your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name and some other personal details about yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Kocaj. I was born on the 7th of November, 1958, in Sarajevo, but I have lived in Vitez all my life, and I still live there. I completed primary and secondary school in Vitez. I graduated in Zagreb at the faculty of economics. After that, I returned to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I am employed in a company there, or rather I was employed until 1991. After that, after the war in Central Bosnia, I was appointed the director of the town library in Vitez, the public library. I am also a correspondent, journalist of Vecernji List, and I also am in literature. I have published three books up to now, and my second book deals with the war in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kocaj. I hope that we have introduced you sufficiently, at least, as regards facts. Can you tell us now, you live in Vitez; when did you meet Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I got to know Vlado Santic when I was 12 years old, so it was around 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you met him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, when he moved into the building next to the one I live in, and so we started associating from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you become friends with Vlado when you were boys?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, we became friends. As soon as he arrived, we simply started keeping company, spontaneously, and that's how it went on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that you had some interests in common at that time which drew you together and on which your friendship was based?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, you could say that we simply felt close as persons, and we kept company the way young people do. We engaged in sports, hiking, and other things we were interested in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what interests Vlado Santic showed at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, Vlado was, I might say, a boy like all of us at that time, but I can say that even then, he knew what he wanted in life. He was more mature than I was, and I still think so today. It was a characteristic of his, this maturity, which is what I remember him by.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What about his attitude towards your other friends that you had in common?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, his attitude to our other friends was always, in my opinion, very correct. He was always kind of protective towards me, perhaps because he was stronger physically and more mature than the rest of us, so it seemed natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: During boyhood, boys sometimes have fights with their peers. Did Vlado show any such aggressive tendencies then?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I never got into fights; it was not a characteristic of mine. And I don't remember Vlado ever getting into a fight, although I'm sure he would have got into one to protect me, if that had been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you saw Vlado as more mature, as a boy who knew what he wanted; do you remember what Vlado chose as his vocation in life?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, after primary school, Vlado went to Sarajevo, to the secondary school for policemen, and that was his vocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was when you separated, probably?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, I can't say we separated, because we spent the weekends together. Sarajevo is not far from Vitez. Vlado did go to school there, but there were weekends, there were summer holidays, winter holidays. So our friendship continued, especially since in the period of secondary school, we used to go hiking in the hills, in the mountains. We would often go to Zabrdze, near Vitez, where there is a mountaineer's cottage. We would also explore a cave on Kruscica. That was something we were very enthusiastic about, so we used to do it almost every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when Vladimir Santic came back from his schooling in Sarajevo to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Vladimir came back from Sarajevo after three years, and I think that he got a job almost at once at the police station. I was still going to the four-year grammar school, and we still kept company, we still saw each other, but at that time, Vlado already had a girlfriend, who is his wife today, and he got married quite early. This shows how mature he was. So his life became different from the kind of life we had had up to then, I had. He wanted to have a family, to get on in his career, be a professional. And all this seemed natural to me, because his maturity was simply a part of his character.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you kept company when he was employed at the police station. Do you know what Vlado was like as an employee, as a worker?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I know well that Vlado wanted to get on in his career as a policeman, which he demonstrated later on when he enrolled into the post-secondary administrative school, and I think that whatever he did, he did professionally. For a time, he was moved from post to post. From a policeman, he became a person in charge of issuing documents, but then he was promoted. He kept being promoted, so he got quite high up. Then I went to Zagreb to study, and then we saw each other less often, because I did not come to Vitez that often until I graduated in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Vlado got married. Did you meet his wife?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I know Vlado's wife quite well because her sister is still a neighbour of mine. So I know the family and I know that she, in her own way, is a mature woman, and I know that -- it seems to me that Vlado is still in love with his wife and that they are soulmates. I think that that was the most important thing to him, apart from his career.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you visit each other?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: We visited each other but not so very often, because I was still unmarried, I was still single, so we had different obligations. I had already got a job in Slobodan Princip Seljo where I was in charge of procurement, and I had less time for a social life, so to say, but we did visit each other from time to time. Vlado had his own obligations, so we did not see each other as often as before but, of course, we didn't stop seeing each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does Vlado Santic have children?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he has sons, two very nice young men, Sasa and Sinesja (phoen). It's a family I know relatively well, and I think that they are just an average Vitez family. There were no scandals associated with the family. They're just a normal, average family from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that you are not married, that you are single -- you were single at that time. So as a single man, were you able to evaluate Vlado's attitude towards his children?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, Vlado's attitude toward his children was -- it's hard to describe. It was fatherly. He was a fatherly authority for his children. His eldest son is of an artistic temperament, and the other one is a typical teenager, and I think that it was a very harmonious family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take you back to the time of the first multi-party elections, the time when national consciousness was awakened and the national feelings came to the fore. Can you tell me, when you recall that time, was Vlado Santic one of those who might be described as becoming nationally conscious at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: As far as I can recall those times in all these events, Vlado Santic's name was never mentioned except as a person working as a professional policeman in the Vitez police station. I cannot say that Vladimir was ever singled out or, rather, that he ever drew attention to himself as a nationalist. I personally wondered whether he would join the HDZ, whether he would stay a member of the SDP, what he was thinking. There was no doubt that he continued doing his job in a professional manner, together with people of different ethnic origin. There was still Serbs and Bosniaks then at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kocaj, since at that time these national feelings became so fervent that they went beyond the bounds of tolerance toward other ethnic groups, did you notice that Vlado ever expressed intolerance toward members of other ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: At the time -- well, in the '90s we would see each other occasionally, and I never felt any marked change in Vlado's views. I never felt any kind of intolerance when he expressed his views on politics or the political events in our country. He did not change his previous views radically. I think he was simply doing his job, trying to do it professionally, the way he had done everything since the end of his schooling, and I think that this is characteristic of the period as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If we were now to glance briefly at 1991 and 1992 and the overall political, social, and economic situation, and if we were to recall the functioning of the government bodies, both the central and the local government, could you tell us very briefly what the prevailing circumstances were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, starting in 1991, things simply started to happen, first of all as a consequence of the war in Croatia, and then as a consequence of everything that was happening in Bosnia, all the political changes, all the misunderstandings and everything else that was happening. Little by little, a kind of ethnic stratification began. A number of economic problems cropped up, and there was a feeling that the government was functioning less and less well. It was harder and harder for the politicians to agree. But until the open conflict broke out, as far as I can remember, if we are talking about Vlado Santic, I have no knowledge of Vlado Santic ever expressing any nationalist views. I think he simply continued doing his job in the police force, according to the regulations and the rules. Everybody in Vitez knows he tried to do his job highly professionally throughout his career, and I remember that he worked with people of different nationalities, different ethnic origins, and I do not believe that any situations ever occurred in which Vlado Santic ever played that kind of role. I think that his goal was simply to do his job professionally and leave politics alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Vlado as a person at that time working in the criminal police. At that highly complex time there were many deviant events, occurrences; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, at that time there were a number of problems, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: At this Court, some witnesses said that Vlado, working in the criminal police and investigating crimes, investigated only those crimes which were perpetrated against Croats and that he had a negligent attitude as a professional towards crimes committed against members of other ethnic groups, especially Muslims. Is that assessment, which some witnesses have put forward before this Court, true in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of Vlado behaving like that, and I do not know on what basis anyone might come to this conclusion. The mechanisms according to which the police functioned were quite clear at the time, and I think that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time the situation became very complex and open clashes began between the Croats and the Muslims. There were various incidents. Can you tell me whether, at that time -- you say Vlado was a professional policeman -- whether at that time, in your conversation was him, you were able to conclude that he was changing his attitude toward members of other ethnic groups, especially Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: At, to be quite honest, we did not see each other as often as before because I was concerned with my family and what I was able to do. I worked for Caritas, then on the radio and television, but I did not notice any changes in Vlado which might lead to his being here before this Court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have just answered the question I was about to ask. So the war is over and you did not hear because the war, unfortunately, is still a frequent topic of conversation today. So did you ever hear that Vlado Santic played a role in this unfortunate war which would lead to his being accused here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Vlado Santic began to be mentioned only when speculations arose with regard to the indictment we saw first in the newspapers. Then it was published, and it was only then that I personally learned that the name of Vlado Santic was being linked to a certain event. Until that time, I had never heard his name ever being connected to a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: Vitez is a small town, including its surroundings, and in small towns everyone knows everything about everybody. If something bad could have been said about Vladimir Santic in such a small town, in such a milieu, and considering your job, you would probably have heard this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I think I would have certainly heard about it, and I think that his name would have been mentioned very often. I think it would have been very difficult for me not to hear about something that had happened in which Vladimir Santic had taken part and for me not to hear about it, the stories going round Vitez. I had no information about anything bad until people started discussing the indictment. I was a little surprised to hear not just "Vladimir," but to hear several of the names mentioned in the indictment in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Kocaj, I would like to ask you to show us the person you have been talking about today in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, Vladimir Santic is sitting to my left, in the last row.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: We may state that the witness recognised Vladimir Santic in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kocaj. I have no further questions at the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Radovic wishes to put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kocaj, I heard from your testimony today that you have written a book about the war in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is that book finished and printed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It has been printed and published. It was published in 1996, if I remember correctly, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I will ask you questions. I would like to know the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: The book is entitled "The Wounded Swan."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can that book only be obtained in the Vitez area, or can we buy it in Zagreb? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I know that it should be available in Zagreb because the publisher is Tonimir (phoen) from Varazdinske Toplice, so it should be available in bookshops in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you wrote this book, does this book contain your subjective view of the events in the Lasva River Valley, or is it based on your research of certain documentation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, I used the chronology of events in the Lasva River Valley as a kind of guideline, but within that, I wrote eight or nine stories which speak in a subjective manner about my experience of the war in the Lasva River Valley and of what happened, first of all, to the Croats, because I was able to see that and experience that. I was able to learn about the suffering of the Croats in the Lasva River Valley. So it is my view of everything I experienced during that year and a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So these are events seen through your eyes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In that book, do you mention certain people and their role in these events?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: In the book, I mentioned certain persons, but in a literary manner, not using their full name. In literature --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we know what literature is. I would just like to know whether you describe the actions of certain persons in these pre-war and wartime events.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And may we know which persons you described?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, let us say in one story, in one of the stories, a character I described was the late Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But as far as I understand, this does not have a historical background; it's your subjective interpretation? Or is it exactly what he did?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, I used real-life events, and then I wrote about them from my viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So on what basis did you establish the actual events? On the basis of documents, or stories that went 'round?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: On the basis of the chronology of events which we had on the radio and television broadcasting station where I worked during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
