utterances.text: So you obtained your knowledge on the basis of those documents which were available to the television?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's one thing, and the other thing is what I experienced personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At which television were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Radio/television Vitez, the local radio and television station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, can you tell me whether you think that on the basis of your book, we could establish something that is true, factually true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I personally believe you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I am Franck Terrier, and I represent the Prosecution here. I shall ask you a few questions, and I do not think I will be very long. But to link up with the questions that Mr. Radovic asked you about the book that you wrote, about the events in the Lasva, did you write a chapter in that book, or a story, that would be describing the events in Ahmici on the 16th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes. In a story, in the beginning of a story, I mention an event and a conversation with a friend, mentioning what happened in Ahmici, where both he and I -- or rather I did feel that we saw it as a -- we in Vitez saw it as a tragic episode which needed to be remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. What impression can your reader derive about this tragic episode in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, the idea, I believe, is quite clear. It says -- it talks about our boys and says that there a crime was committed, and I think -- I'm not sure if I'm quoting my sentence correctly, but I'm saying that this is a heavy burden, this is a leaden burden on our souls, and it will remain so. This is something that I write about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But this idea about Ahmici, is it your personal statement or the result of -- the product of conversations of meetings that you had with various people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: To begin with, after I learned what had happened in Ahmici and after, I talked to a number of rank-and-file people in Vitez. I think that -- yes, we felt it was a disgrace, and I believe that Croats were having a hard time to come to terms with it. It was rather a taboo topic, and people were rather reluctant to talk about it, I suppose because they felt ashamed, they felt shamed that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this is a crime, you say. Do you have any idea who might have committed the crime? I'm not asking you the names of individual persons, but the unit responsible for it, the chain of command, the kinds of units, military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think that we're now getting into examination about facts; that is, the events that took place there. That is my feeling. If the witness begins to answer this question -- and as far as I know, this week, my colleague Susak also tried to examine a character witness as to facts, and there was an intervention then. I believe we are dealing with a similar situation, so will my learned friend from the Prosecution please confine himself to questions -- that is, answers about matters that this witness has been called upon to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, that he wrote a book about that war, and it therefore seemed to me important to ask him about what this book writes about. Of course, we bear in mind that this is a literary work, and of course -- I mean, that is that kind of witness. I mean, he wrote about these things, simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So will you please answer my question? I was asking you if you, as the author of this book, if you held a certain idea, a certain view about the process, about actions which produced that crime, the unit which was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I shall begin by answering the second part of your question. I really do not know who committed the crime. We all, today, especially, know or learned that it was Croats, or rather Croat soldiers. What units, what uniforms they were, I do not know. And that is something that we are having, both me and other people in Vitez, are finding very hard, because of the nature of that crime. What you asked me about the chain of command and things, I really can't answer that. I could only speculate, bearing in mind the whole chain of events, the series of events before that, that eventually resulted in what happened in Ahmici and the way it happened. But I'm afraid we would be getting into some sociopsychological waters, not to mention the whole genesis of the conflict in Central Bosnia, from the conflict in 1992 to Dusina in January 1993, and so on and so forth. I'm not sure that you really want me to answer your question in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, Witness, certainly not. I expected a simpler answer. This is a crime, and crimes usually lead to some investigation, and that is the only reason why I asked the question. But your friend, Vlado Santic, who was a member of the Croat community and an HVO officer and a policeman, didn't he somehow respond or react to that crime, to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, I can answer you that question in the following way: During the war, I do not think I ever met Vlado Santic during the war except in 1994 -- or rather 1995, when we met by chance, and that was the first time that we had time for a chat of some duration, so I did mention that crime. As far as I can recall, Vlado Santic showed that he was thinking along similar lines, and he said something that I really hoped I would hear from him. He also said that he believed it was a war crime and that somebody would have to be called to account for it, and that is what I think about it too. And I don't really know what else to say. Perhaps, if you rephrase your question, perhaps I might answer it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But could you tell us more specifically during which period of time you did not see your friend Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I did not see him in 1993 and the first half of '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1993, that is, in April, what were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: In '93, I was already with the Vitez radio/television and was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a journalist, what field did you cover? What area of activity did you cover?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: I had a programme which was called "Loose Goods," and it was a collage. There was a little bit of information, a little bit of politics, some entertainment, and a features part which would cover the developments, by and large, the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the principal thing. And secondly, I performed all the journalistic tasks; that is, writing the local news, various greetings, listeners' wishes, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And did you, at any time, hold a responsible position in any of the institutions in any of the establishments representing the Croat community?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Sometime, if I remember properly, sometime in the summer of '93, when the director of radio/television, Slavko Pavlovic, retired, then I took over the post of the manager of the radio/television there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please -- this is not an exhibit for the Prosecution, and I am not tendering it. This is a document, and I want the witness to explain something to me, simply. That is all. Mr. Usher, will you please give it to the Chamber and also place a copy of it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look at the bottom and to the left on this document; tell us if this is your name and your signature to the left. Witness, you can look directly, because you don't have it on your monitor, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes, at the bottom, to the left, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please explain? What is this about? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: At that time, I volunteered as the secretary of the employers' cooperative, which was formed in Vitez, I believe, in October '93, and I am still the secretary of the employers' cooperative in Vitez, still a volunteer. And as far as I remember, this document was to show where people worked during a particular period of time. I notice here the name of Josipa Bracic, and I can't remember other names, but this was simply to certify that such-and-such people were employed by the employers' cooperative. It was needed for some records -- what do you call it -- the Ministry of Defence, or whatever it's called. I don't really remember what that particular body is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And my last question, if I may: You told us that your friend Vlado Santic, as a policeman, behaved very correctly, professionally, and impartially, but you also said that you did not have any precise information as to how he operated in his professional performance, that you did not have any information about his professional performance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Excuse me, but what period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992/93.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: In 1992 -- well, it is not that I didn't have any information, any knowledge for the whole year, but as of November 1992, I really wasn't coming across Vlado Santic any more, for objective reasons. I remember the family, and I was simply devoting myself to the family and things that I was doing at the time. That was the -- what I would call a leaden time, the time of political upheaval, political unrest, and I really did not feel like going out and socialising with anyone. I didn't simply think it was a propitious time for that. I'm not a particularly brave man, and I prefer family life, I must say, to some activities, so I just performed my professional work, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, but, Witness, didn't you even talk on the telephone or just meet anywhere with Vlado Santic? Isn't it paradoxical, after all, that at some moment the circumstances become very difficult, the tension mounts, and at that particular moment you -- I do not say that you break, but you are simply not seeing your close and old friend any more. Doesn't that sound -- isn't that a little bit curious?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't see why should it be a surprise. Simply we were both too busy to meet too often. At such a time you don't really think very much about going out, about hanging out. Nobody feels like going out, or at least I did not feel like that. I worked at the radio and television. I spent there 12, 16 hours sometimes if it was necessary. I was doing my job and I was going home. I had a small child, and I wanted to spend as much time as possible with him and my wife. So we were not seeing many people at the time except for our next-door neighbours. As soon as the night would fall there were problems on the road, as soon as it grew dark, so why would one go out? Information about what I wanted to know, I more or less had this information. I came from Vitez. I knew what things looked like. I do not see anything paradoxical, simply it was life and we just parted our ways for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it was not the differences of opinion or differences of attitude that drove you apart?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KOCAJ
utterances.text: No. We simply did not happen to meet. The situations of life in the wartime separated us. I presume he had his own obligations and duties and he did them the way he did them, and I had my own. There was simply no time for this kind of informal meetings, socialising, going out together, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I have no more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions. Mr. Kocaj, thank you so much for giving evidence in Court. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration? Good morning would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, witness.

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Court, first?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Marko Brkovic. I was born on the 23rd of October, 1942, in the village of Has, the municipality of Novi Travnik, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be of interest if you told us about Has, your birthplace. What would that mean if we wish to translate that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Has or Hus is a Muslim settlement with a dual origin. Hus means "the biggest" in Turkish. Has means "impure, filthy."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having enlightened us or, sorry, at least myself. Well, tell me then, Mr. Brkovic, could you please tell us which schools you attended?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I attended the first four grades of elementary school in my native village, and after that I continued my education in Bugojno. Bugojno is about 100 kilometres away from my native village. At that time, it was difficult to obtain an education because this was the immediate post-war period. After the Second World War, things were difficult and my father bought a farm near Bugojno and that's where I continued my schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkovic, after that did you attend university and what did you study?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I completed high school in Bugojno, and then I continued my university studies in Sarajevo where I graduated from the academy of pedagogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So this meant you went to a teachers' college? Is that what it means, broadly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Brkovic, when did you first get a job and what was that job?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I did what I was trained to do, that is to say, to teach elementary school. In 1964, starting on the 1st of September, 1964, I found a job in Busovaca, the municipality of Busovaca, because I had obtained a scholarship from them earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were involved in teaching. Were you head teacher in one of those classes or perhaps did you become principal of some school or what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the law that was in force at that time, schools are educational institutions, that is to say, it was the duty of every teacher, in addition to teaching his subjects, to work on the education and upbringing of pupils. In order to do that, he was supposed be the head-class teacher so he would know the structure and forms of communicating with children so as to help and facilitate their development.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So let us go back to those days, and if I ask you if the name of Nada Santic means something to you, what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: After I worked in Busovaca for three years, I went to the area of Romanija, Han-Piejsak namely, and then I spent a brief period there. Then I came to the territory of the municipality of Vitez. I taught in elementary school of Bila, four kilometres out of the town of Vitez. That's where I found a job as a teacher of mathematics and physics, and I became a home-room teacher for an 8th grade class. Since I had worked in a high school before that, I knew what these 8th Graders were supposed to face once they left elementary school and went to high school, they were adolescents, and this was very important. One of my pupils in this class was Nada Santic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you pay visits to the parents of this student of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Not only the parents of that particular pupil but of all other pupils. A teacher, an educator, is duty-bound to familiarise himself with the structure, education, background, et cetera, of all students and their families, and all of this is highly relevant. I visited the parents of Nada Santic, but before that I visited other parents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: As home-room teacher, I was supposed to fill out a form and certain details had to be entered there that were sought by the school or, rather, the Ministry of Education, because it is the Ministry of Education that had prescribed that form. When I met the Santic family, we would usually pay group visits. I mean, a group of teachers, a group of my colleagues would go, and that is when I went to meet Mirko, the father, Lucija the mother, the sister, and also the young boy Vlado whom I didn't know him then but I got to know him in 5th Grade because I came together with his home-room teacher Josip Silic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is when you met the young Vlado. Are you referring to Vlado Santicic, and you came here to testify on his behalf today? You were asked by us to do so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about something from that period? What was the attitude of Vlado's parents, to the best of your knowledge, towards him and the rest of their children, the brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, by way of comparison, as we visited other parents in the immediate neighbourhood, as we were filling out these forms we were supposed to get to know people well, that is to say, what kind of a home they had, how well off they were, whether the school was supposed to give them some kind of subsidy or whether the school was supposed to provide supplementary meals to the children and what kind of education the parents had, et cetera. Some pupils I had visited, because I was not familiar with the environment at the time, did not have a radio or a television or any conditions for work. In the Santic family I found a completely different situation. This was a civilised family where the children had a study of their own. They had a TV set, a radio, a library of their own. They had well-kept books. They had plenty of space to study. They had all amenities. So they had truly civilised conditions for pursuing a regular education.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you have just told us, can we conclude that they were a rich family?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not a rich family. They were modestly rich. Now, what do I mean by that? They were focused on creating the right conditions for a proper education for their children, and things were rather difficult sometimes and conditions were modest. There were people who were jobless. Sometimes people were considered to be rich even if they owned a bicycle only. So you cannot really talk about wealth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what you have said, you're obviously a person who can pass relevant judgement on such relationships. If you recall these conversations that you had with the parents, how did they see their children? What are the kind of values that they wanted to instil in them? What did they actually want their children to become in the future?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We wrote down what we saw. These parents lived for the future of their children. They had sufficient conditions for providing a proper education for the education of their children. No one drank, no one smoked in that family, and nothing could have affected the children in an adverse way. The parents were very caring and loving, and they developed the right kind of relationships with their children. The oldest child was the one that was in charge of the younger siblings, so to speak. That is to say, their oldest child Nada acted as a teacher acts in school, checking on her younger siblings and seeing whether that they had done everything that they were supposed to do for school. The parents were highly interested in everything, because they came to school regularly and they wanted to find out how their children were doing, what kind of grades they had, what kind of company they kept, whether they had any difficulties, whether they were helping others as they were, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When Vlado grew up and when he went to school, when he was a big boy and when he started school, you were his teacher; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A year later, after I arrived there, I taught Vlado physics. I was his teacher. I was not his home-room teacher, but I was his physics teacher. This was the school year of 1969/1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How did Vlado Santic behave in school but apart from actual classes in terms of extra-curricular behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In my career I had quite a few students so singling out students is not really the right thing to do, but the Santic family was well liked by us because of Nada who was one of my best students. She took part in competitions in mathematics and physics. She represented our school, and I simply expected quite a few things from her brother. I expected him to be a very good physicist too. He liked history, he liked biology, but he would not take part in physics competitions. Well, as far as Vlado's attitude is concerned, I think that he started school a bit too early. You can see that only when they start moving on to senior grades and when they start studying more difficult, more complex subjects. He was a very good student. He was not super talented for physics though, but he was super talented for something else. Among his colleagues, among his friends, to the best of my recollection, he was very well liked. He liked his colleagues, they liked him. They watched sports games together, because he was one of the very few children to have a TV set at home, and we, the men, would often comment on this. He was friends with children from his immediate neighbourhood because there were the Savanovic, Varupa, Zolota families, et cetera. They were always in the same group and there was never any kind of excessive behaviour in that group. There were no problems. There was nothing else that was characteristic in a negative sense. I wish to point this out because there were quite a few of those who were poor. There were those who did not even have enough food. Vlado was one who would help such children. They would collect money. When somebody needed a book and could not afford it, he would collect money for such a child. Especially if somebody's parents would die, then Vlado would be one of those who would collect money for wreaths and flowers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said at that time Vlado was very well liked by his peers. Was he prepared to help them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that everything I mentioned shows what a humane person he was, what a faithful and loyal person he was and that other pupils liked him. I noticed that especially when Vlado was leaving our school, because everybody wanted, at all costs, to part with him. And I think that this was a very sad day for him when he left and when he went to Vitez, because his father, having been an outstanding worker, had obtained an apartment and he went to this other job and this other apartment and Vlado left our school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did Vlado live at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when he left our school, he moved into an urban environment, and he lived in my own neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about Vlado as a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I knew the parents quite well and the pupils, now our relationship grew into a neighbourly relationship. We were neighbours who knew each other well, and they were ready to acknowledge the elderly and to be helpful. This is something I particularly liked. Vlado always behaved to me as if he were still my student. I consulted his colleagues, and I asked whether Vlado still enjoyed the kind of authority like the one he did while he was at our school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When we were preparing ourselves for this conversation, and when we were recalling these subjects, you told me that you would often monitor your former pupils' progress further on, even after they left your school. What could you say about Vlado Santic in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is something that is characteristic of psychology, just as a coach monitors his players and a priest his parishioners. That is how a teacher feels about his pupils. So a teacher's love for his pupils continues and it grows into a different relationship based on mutual respect. That is the kind of relationship I had with Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Vlado Santic chose to be a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the times that we were living in at that time, in the '70s, there was an unemployment crisis in our town. There were a large number of young people who completed school and who could not find a job. At that time, the Ministry of Interior had public competitions inviting young people to join their ranks and offering them scholarships, and they would get uniforms and a proper job after they completed their education. So that was probably his motive. Before he went to school, I talked about this both to Vlado and his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Until Vlado left Vitez in 1977, were you in touch with him afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: With Vlado Santic? I was in constant contact with him. We had a cooperation. When he completed the police academy, he came as a young policeman. I was so pleased. It was an honour for me to have one of my former students in the police. I had one of my own, so to speak, there. Vlado was the youngest policeman I had seen in my life. He looked as if he were only 15 years old. Perhaps he was 18 or 19. I do not recall having ever seen a younger policeman. Very soon he started to work on the road as a traffic policeman. I never heard Vlado, as a policeman, using swear words, I never saw him smoking, I never saw him beating up other people as was customary in the case of others. I know that he was active in the auto motor club. He also married when he was very young. I was invited to his party, and he said that he would continue his studies and that he would get a degree in law, which he did, and very quickly at that. He worked on the issuing of IDs and other documents, and that was very important. You see, when you come and when you have lots of people waiting in a queue in front of you, like 30 people or something, it's very important to have one of your own, so that you don't have to wait, and that's important. We also organised in school various competitions, and they had to do with traffic and the knowledge of traffic signs, et cetera. Traffic accidents can be very dangerous, and Vlado was the one who brought traffic signs and distributed them in schools, in public places, and he organised the school competition, the municipal competition, the republican competition, national, international, world championship. So there were lots, really. I also worked in the fire brigade with Vlado, and he worked on the protection of human lives and property as president of the fire brigade, and I, as his former teacher, lectured on the danger of fires, especially Poculica, Bukve, and many other places. That was indispensable, and it turned out to be very useful, and human lives were saved in the way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Pavkovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkovic, I would now like to channel your attention to the events of 1990, 1991, the multi-party elections. I would like to know how you saw Vlado within the scope of those events.

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the '90s, Vlado was working in the criminal police. I was the principal of the school at that time, and to speak of that period means to speak of the prevailing political situation at the time, and he as a policeman and I as the principal of a school had, so to say, subsidiary roles. I noticed Vlado at rallies to which I was supposed to bring pupils. They were supposed to carry flags, flowers, and so on. As far as I can remember, Vlado did not take part in those rallies as a citizen, but only professionally, as a policeman, because these were rallies at which various kinds of people with various views were present, and he was there as a policeman, in a professional capacity, trying to protect citizens, to maintain law and order, and to do everything he had been doing previously as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me something about his standpoints in relation to members of other ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado was born in a mixed environment. In his neighbourhood there were people who were orthodox Serbs, who were Roma, Muslims, and others. I never noticed or saw or felt that Vlado had a different attitude toward them than he had toward those of his own nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So in those years, perhaps I'm not expressing myself properly, but it was a time of national euphoria. Did Vlado succumb to that kind of euphoric feelings?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can say that he did not. I never saw him drunk. I never saw him insulting or humiliating others or demeaning the value of other people. He always worked on creating a healthy environment. He always acted professionally, and then he always came back to his family. In the former system, the central government was then becoming very weak, so the police force had a major job to do in maintaining law and order and protecting citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the Muslims and his attitude toward Muslims, as you said, it was a mixed environment in which he was born and grew up; did he show any kind of intolerance, or even hatred, toward that community?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, and I am convinced, knowing him, that this was not so. I will give you a few examples. In 1991, when the central government was weakened, many institutions came under attack. There were burglaries, and this happened in my school. Vlado was working in the criminal police. He was working on finding these burglars and thieves. When I called the police, Vlado came, and I wanted him to come. He never asked me, "Was this done by a Croat, a Muslim, or a Serb?" He always said, "It was a thief who did this. Thieves have no religion and no nationality; they are simply thieves." So Vlado was not a person who drew distinctions among people on the basis of their ethnic origin. He drew distinctions on the basis of whether they were honest or whether they were thieves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkovic. I will conclude my examination with some brief questions about Vlado's family. I assume you know something about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Vlado is married; you know that he has children?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what his attitude was toward his family and his children?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the educational system, there are three ways in which children are brought up: at home, by society, and in the street. In this family, the children were brought up at home. Just as Mirko Santic, Vlado Santic's father, tried to raise his children, Vlado followed his father's example and was a very caring and loving father, doing his best to raise his children. I got to know his wife, Mrs. Slavica Josipovic (sic). I knew her father, who was a forester and who cooperated with our school in renewing the woods. This was a modest family in which there were never any insults or fights. This was a family which knew how to distinguish good from evil and which knew how to raise its children properly. I was very happy to hear that Vlado had married someone from that family. And when he had two sons, I got to know his children too. I was very happy that he had children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about Slavica Josipovic as Vlado's wife; Josipovic is her maiden name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brkovic, this is my last question. You say that you got to know Vlado's children?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What can you say about them today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as the principal of the school, when the war ended, the schools organised competitions in all subjects for the Vitez municipality. And when, as the school principal, I came after the first term -- and this started late, because of the war -- when I came to the exhibition of pupils' work, we had several pupils who were very talented. One of them stood out in drawing, in art, and when I looked at his name, I saw that it was Sasa Santic, the son of Vlado Santic. I approached him. He won the first prize as the youngest talented artist, and we all congratulated him warmly. Then, at Easter, there was an exhibition organised at the level of the Vitez municipality, and he participated with his paintings and was highly acclaimed. I was very happy about this, because he was the son of one of my pupils. I went to his home to congratulate him, and he presented me with several of his paintings, which I still keep as souvenirs, as mementoes. I knew that at that time the financial situation was very bad, so I did my best to make it possible for him to go to the academy of fine arts, and he was one of the youngest and most talented students. When I asked him whether he could go to university, he said, "Drawing is what relaxes me, but law is what refreshes me." He is studying at two faculties at the university simultaneously, and he is the only student from Vitez who is doing so. He is to be congratulated, because he has given up all other forms of entertainment and devoted himself exclusively to his studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And he has another son whom you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This other son is also a very clever child. He is also at university, and I think that there are no problems as regards his studies. I don't know what his financial situation is, but I hope that he will succeed. As regards his talents, I think that he is in love with books.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to take this opportunity to tender into evidence the following Defence exhibit. It is a certificate issued to illustrate some of the facts mentioned. It is from the police administration of Vitez, showing the address where Vlado Santic lived, that he lived in Vitez for a certain period of time. I would also like to tender the police certificate from Vitez showing that Vlado Santic has no criminal record. I would also like to tender three entries into the birth register relating to Vlado Santic's sons and his marital status. I would like to ask the usher to take this set of documents for the Trial Chamber and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The certificate of the police of Vitez, with the Vladimir Santic address, will be D13/6. A police certificate saying that Mr. Vladimir is not under criminal investigation is D14/6. The birth certificate and the marriage certificate will be D15/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There are no objections, so they are admitted into evidence. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm Franck Terrier, and I represent the Prosecution in this case. A moment ago you described the young pupil, Vlado Santic. You knew him at the time as a student. You told us that he was a very industrious, diligent student, and so on and so forth. Would you also say that Vlado Santic had a very strong personality, a very strong character, ever since his childhood, or perhaps had some leadership ambitions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wouldn't say so. He was not a leader. He could not be a leader because he wasn't the strongest, he wasn't the brightest, he wasn't the best off. But others liked him, others respected him, and he was humane. In school, a leader in school is usually somebody who is the strongest, perhaps who has the strongest personality, and of course, in senior classes, the handsomest one. It depends in what way he is a leader: Does he charm all the girls, or is he the leader of a sports section, or anything like that. But he was not a leader. He was very attractive. He was a very merry fellow, very attractive, he was humane, and he did not strike one as a leader. He struck one as a modest man, to help, to promote, to help those who have no means of livelihood, who have nothing to write with, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, another witness, the witness before you, told us that Vlado Santic had big, important professional ambitions, and he said that he was an ambitious police officer. Would you corroborate that statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado Santic was a very gifted person; there is no dilemma about that. And he proved it because he was one of the youngest policeman, as I have said, that I have seen. However, one needs to bear in mind the time and the space in which Vlado became a policeman. At that time, there were working in the police people who were under-educated, who had already been spent, who had come from somewhere else. Vlado came from this milieu where he was born, and that is where he appeared as a policeman. He was very ambitious, because immediately after graduating from police school -- that is, passing his trainee test -- he was immediately promoted to a policeman in the street, and he became a traffic warden. He regulated the traffic, and after that he enrolled in the faculty and also graduated within the deadline, with very high marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us also about a ceremony to which you took your children. The ceremony, if I understood you properly, was of somewhat of a political nature. Vlado Santic was present, you told us, in his capacity as a police officer. What was that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, 1992, many political rallies were organised. Those were the promotions of individual parties which had been established, and the school, as a public institution, was bound to add to the importance of these rallies by their presence. That is, we as a school were bound to bring the children, when invited by individual parties, because children could be amused there, there was entertainment, and of course they would be offered some meats or something. Of course, I did not attend the ceremonies in the same capacity as Vlado. Being principal of the school, I was bound to organise the presence of our pupils at those rallies, and Vlado was there to ensure law and order. However, our encounters, whether deliberate or perchance, were always cordial, and there were quite a number of such meetings, of such rallies, and most of them were of an entertaining nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What political party are you referring to, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were political parties from SDP, HDZ, SDA, and many political parties which held their publicity meetings. That was that kind of life then, and these were meetings that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in 1991, 1992, representatives of those political parties asked you to bring all the children to attend these political events?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not have to take all children. Some older children, because their school was four kilometres away from the centre of town, and children were also free. If the meetings were organised on working days, the school was bound to organise the attendance of children at those rallies at the invitation of the official authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That is as of what age were the children requested to attend political rallies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were senior grades of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you specify the age of those people in elementary school grades?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Those are children over the age of 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about how often did you meet with Vlado Santic during, shall we say, between the time of elections in 1992 until 1993? Did you meet often and how often?

utterances.speaker: MARKO BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not meet often. There were official -- that is, in 1992, in the school which I was the principal, the United Nations forces came to our school. In 1991, we met in passing because we lived very near one another. In 1992, there was an incident, that is, the International forces which came to my school, and I was their host for two months, and they asked me to introduce them to the political representatives of the town and the police representatives, and I then introduced Vlado to those representatives. There was also a theft precisely at the time they came because some things disappeared. Then Vlado came with the police team for an intervention, and they paid tribute to him because that object which had been alienated was then returned within the shortest possible time. So the policemen in the police department that was represented, that the criminal department, would drop by every now and then, ask questions, and wanted to be helpful, wanted to be at hand both for me and them, but me principally as their host, until my departure, that is, until moved out of the school. Furthermore, at that time there were many shortcomings. Some people turned up whom I did not know. They were armed and I was fearing for my pupils. Very often classes would be discontinued because of some detonations or some -- and the school was also exposed to the mountain of Vlasic, and on it were deployed some units which often opened fire. So that during one school year the classes had to be interrupted two or three times. In order to protect the pupils, I went to the police quite often to inquire whether I should discontinue the classes, and I also often turned to Vlado Santic, at the criminal department, and who told me, "If need be, you will be notified. Rest assured. Trust us. We shall do everything within our power to assure the safety of those children." I really trusted him, when Vlado told me that we did not need to be afraid. I trusted him and I did not interrupt the classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no additional questions, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if you are releasing the witness. I have to say something. The counsel, rather, Defence has completed the production of evidence. In conclusion, I would like to turn to evidence -- certified statements of five individuals who gave their statements in accordance with Rule 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But meanwhile, I will tell the witness that we are thankful to you, Mr. Brkovic, for coming to the Hague to give evidence in Court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please take care of these documents? I'll hand them over to the Chamber and for the Prosecution. These are the statements by Muharem Pripoljac, Nesada Calic, Nada Josipovic, Slavica Santic, and Miro Lazarevic. I should like to introduce them all as one exhibit, one Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did you mention, Counsel Pavkovic, Rule 93?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't think so. I believe it is 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 94 ter. Affidavits. These are affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no. I'm referring to character statements of witnesses, and this is Rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 94 ter. 94 ter, yes. These are affidavits. This is in compliance with our request. You don't have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, no. I have five days to object. No. No. I only have one comment. So far documents were handed over either on the eve of the testimony. Now Mr. Pavkovic is giving us documents at the very last moment. We here have a series of documents that is a series of affidavits. We naturally have no time to even look at them. So I have no objections but on the reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friends. I did not want to deny you any information. You will see these are statements which are strictly related to the personality of Vlado Santic. They are not dealing with absolutely -- to any event absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Prosecutor will have a few days before saying whether or not they object to this particular document. It will be what, D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness statement of Muharem Pripoljac will be D16/6. Nesada Calic, D17/6. Statement by Nada Josipovic will be D18/6. The statement by Slavica Santic will be D19/6. Miro Lazarevic's statement will be D20/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I also tender two statements relative to Dragan Papic's character? They are by Drago Krizanovic and Drago Pranjes. I believe that this will be consistent with your decision of 11th of February, 1999, under Rule 94 ter of the Rules. We showed it to the Prosecution some 20 days ago, I believe, and the Prosecutor has told us they have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Will the usher please help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No objections. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So, therefore, these two documents will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement of Drago Pranjes will be D21/ (sic) ... and the statement of Mr. Nikola Krizanovic will be D30/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, D29 and D30/5. For the record, it is D29/5 and D30/5. All right. Before we adjourn, let me ask -- yes, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I shall be very brief. Drago Josipovic's Defence, on the 17th of February, 1999, submitted a motion asking the Prosecution to submit all the statements of the Defence of Drago Josipovic for Mirsad Omserovic. After that, the Chamber, on the 2nd of March, 1999, passed a decision ordering, among other things, that the Prosecution should disclose the whole Annex 5 with the exception of the names of the investigators and the first line, the first fragment, and two sentences in that document. In view that after that the Chamber decided that other annexes, from 1 to 4, do not relate to exculpatory evidence, whereas Annex 5 was said to be exculpatory evidence. I believe that the Trial Chamber should order the Prosecutor to submit to the Defence Annex 5 without deleted places, that is, the witnesses who testified here saying that it was not Mirsad Omserovic or Mirsad Osmanac, as it is stated in all the Prosecutor's papers and his notes and it would, therefore, be very useful if Annex 5 were handed over to the Defence without any pieces stricken out so we could establish who that document is about, Mirsad Osmanac or Mirsad Omserovic or who else. To this date, the Prosecutor has yet not disclosed about the person in question, who they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you wish a comment from us on this point? I think I can be of some assistance to you, probably to my friend Mr. Susak. The bottom line is that there was every suspicion on the part of Mr. Susak, which we looked into as well, that the note made in the name of Omserovic referred directly to Mirsad Osmancevic. The brief facts that were recorded seemed on all fours with the facts recorded in a note relating to Osmancevic. I think we can probably take that as read. They are one and the same person. The Annex 5 to the motion we submitted under Rule 67 or 66(C), my memory fails me at the moment, Your Honours, was to disclose all forms of relevant paperwork, and you were able to see all of it in the naked raw and determine what was appropriate, if anything, by way of redaction. I am sure -- well, I can say from memory and maybe Your Honours can too, that the Annexure 5 that was revealed and disclosed in a slightly more expanded form than the original notation by the Prosecution, disclosed everything that was relevant to the person and anything redacted would in no way have assisted Mr. Susak in tracing or contacting the said Osmancevic. After that there was an oral request in this Chamber, and we said -- in fact, I said that although our files had been exhaustively checked, and I understood Your Honours to be satisfied that we'd done everything, we had no further relevant information, we made an inquiry of the Bosnian authorities, the results of which were known only a brief time ago. It was at some point in the course of last week. During that time, we had investigators in the field, and I will tell Your Honours and Mr. Susak that those investigators requested Mr. Osmancevic be contacted by those authorities. Would he speak to the Defence or indeed would he speak to anybody? The response was in the negative and, as a result, in fact, he wouldn't even grant any kind of contact with our own people, let alone would he grant contact either with the Defence. It wasn't a partisan decision, it was a total decision on his part. We're, therefore, faced with that position. Yesterday we did file a brief motion ex parte to Your Honours to consider one particular further aspect. I won't mention that any further, but subject to Your Honours' ruling, we're naturally concerned for the protection of the -- of any potential victims or witnesses involved in cases, and obviously it is a matter we seek Your Honours' guidance at this time. Other than that, we really have done, I think, all that we can. I can say that the evidence so for adduced in respect of Mr. Osmancevic, his sheltering at the house of Anto Papic and the use of this military vest for safe travel to Ravno and back, these are not facts which we have in contention, so we are not contesting that evidence adduced by the Defence. So I hope that's of some assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed it is correct what the Prosecutor just said. Some time ago we did take a look at Annex 5. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. You did take a look at it. I'm talking about Annexes 1 to 4, because they do not relate to exculpatory evidence. However, I do not understand what the Prosecutor did. He did not give us the name and surname of Mirsad Osmancevic and his occupation, because many witnesses said that he was a member of the BH army, and I don't see really why we should have these blanks in this document and not to allow the Defence to see this introductory part of the material concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I recall the redactions and that, there were such things as the title given to the document and, I believe, the name of the investigator, and certainly parts relating, as I recall, to profession and address were blank, not so much redacted. There simply was no entry there. Again, we don't contest that if it said this man is a member of the BiH army. We don't contest that as a matter of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. We were given all these documents. We did not find anything of relevance for the Defence. So that's why we ruled that they were not important or relevant to the Defence. As I say, since the Prosecutor does not contest the facts as adduced by Counsel Susak, we don't see why they should be handed over to the Defence. So I think as for Annex 5, again we are satisfied that the Prosecutor has complied with the duties incumbent upon the Prosecution, and that the question raised by the Defence is not in dispute because again the Prosecutor admits -- they agree that this man, Osmancevic, was given safe passage to Ravno and was given a military vest to go there. So the facts or not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, my learned friend the Prosecutor then agrees with me that this is Mirsad Osmancevic in Annex 5, that he is a Muslim by nationality and that he's a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think I've already agreed those points indeed, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. Very well. Thank you, Counsel Susak. So we may do some planning for next week. Next week we will start with the court witness, the anthropologist, and then I understand that you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, will call a witness, the one we mentioned before. What else? Shall we move then to the accused? So probably then on Tuesday we will start with, I assume, Zoran Kupreskic, then Mirjan, and then Vlatko. All right. Any questions? Any problems? So next week we will be sitting from 9.00 to 1.15. Yes. We will be sitting from 9.00 to 1.15 because Judge May is sitting in another case in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just one thing. I wonder if Mr. Pavkovic had any news about Mr. Marin. We'd left the issue yesterday that he was going to try and find out why he hadn't come. It might affect the running order of next week, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I do not have any news. Yesterday I had to deal with all these topical issues at hand, and later on, if I deem it necessary, I'm going to call Mr. Marin and I'm going to inform the court of this, and I believe that this is my right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So we will know later on. You said that you will later on decide whether you deem it necessary to call him if he's prepared to come over to the Hague. You will decide. It's for you to decide. If you decide for the negative, namely not to call him as a witness, then I wonder whether the Prosecution is keen to call him for cross-examination. We just wanted to suggest that there may be a problem, but we can come back to this problem later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, we should like to cross-examine this witness. He's expected to come to corroborate the Defence alibis. We simply cannot accept the witness explanation that was given to the Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, Slavko Marin is a military man. I asked the military authorities for their approval for him to come here. Before my departure for The Hague, I did not receive any word from them. They did not refuse my request, but they did not grant it either. So I really have to look into this matter. I don't know any more today than I did yesterday. I'm going to do my best to inform the Prosecutor and the Court, in time, if and when I find something out, and if -- for us, the Defence, his arrival would be of consequence and, of course, if the Prosecutor believes it is of importance to him, well and fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may say so, the ball is in Mr. Pavkovic's court, but another question to which we did not receive any answer is whether the witness has deposed. Perhaps the question is premature. Perhaps we shall be asking it later on, but the question is whether the absence of Slavko Marin might affect the deposition of the accused in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic, have you made up your mind about whether or not the accused, your client, will give evidence in Court or does it depend on this particular witness, Slavko Marin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, now that we have concluded our evidence, I'm going to look into the situation with my client, and then we're going to agree on what we're going to do both in relation to Slavko Marin and in relation to his very own appearance, that of the accused. I'm going to do as I told you a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Of course, I mean if you come across any problem, we could be requested to subpoena this particular witness so that the military authorities will have to comply with our request. We may subpoena him so that he has got to come, if you consider that he is a crucial witness. All right? We may adjourn now until Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 1.00 p.m. to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of July, 1999 at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
